title: Expiring Key Cache
statement:
Build a key–value cache where every entry has a time to live, like an HTTP response cached with max-age. An entry written at time now with lifetime ttl is alive at every time t with t < now + ttl, and gone from now + ttl on.

Real code would read a clock. So tests can replay a timeline, every method here takes the current time now (in milliseconds) as its first argument instead. Times never decrease from one call to the next.

  • ExpiringCache() creates an empty cache.
  • set(now, key, value, ttl) stores value under key with a fresh lifetime, replacing any older value and lifetime. It returns true if the key had an alive entry just before this call, otherwise false.
  • get(now, key) returns the value if the key's entry is alive, otherwise -1.
  • count(now) returns how many keys have an alive entry.

Tests are a list of operations and their arguments; the first creates the cache. The output has one entry per operation (null for the constructor).

examples.why: The entry lives for times 0 … 99. At exactly 100 it is gone.
The second set finds key 1 alive and returns true. It also restarts the lifetime: the entry now lives until 80, not 50.
At time 10 the first entry has just expired, so the second set reports false, even though the key is still sitting in the map.

hints: Store each key's value together with the time it stops being alive. That alone answers set and get.
count is the hard one: scanning every key is too slow when there are many. Which entries do you need to throw out at time now?
Keep a min-heap of (expiry, key). Before answering, pop every heap entry with expiry ≤ now and delete the key if the map still holds that same expiry. Then count is just the map's size.

explain.intuition:
Each key keeps its value and its expiry time now + ttl. get and set just compare now with that stored expiry. Because "alive" depends on the time, an expired entry may still sit in the map. That is harmless for get, but count would have to check every key.

Instead, clean up as time moves forward, the same way a browser cache evicts stale entries lazily. A min-heap ordered by expiry always shows the next entry to die. Before each call, pop everything that has expired. An overwritten key leaves an old heap entry behind; when it surfaces, the map's expiry no longer matches it, so you skip it. After the cleanup the map holds exactly the alive keys, and count is its size.
steps: Keep map: key → (value, expiry) and a min-heap of (expiry, key).
purge(now): while the heap's smallest expiry is ≤ now, pop it; if the map's entry for that key has exactly that expiry, delete the key.
set: purge, note whether the key is in the map, store (value, now + ttl), push to the heap, return the note.
get: purge, then return the stored value or -1.
count: purge, then return the map's size.
pitfalls: Treating an entry as alive at exactly now + ttl. Example 1 needs -1 at time 100.
Answering set with "is the key in the map?" without checking expiry. Example 3 has an expired entry still stored.
Deleting a key when an old heap entry for it pops, after the key was rewritten with a later expiry. Compare the popped expiry with the stored one first.

solutions.title: Map with expiry, count by scanning
solutions.idea: Store value and expiry per key. get and set compare times directly; count walks every stored key.
solutions.time: O(1) for set and get, O(n) for count

solutions.title: Map plus a min-heap of expiries
solutions.idea: Evict lazily in expiry order before every call. Stale heap entries from overwritten keys are recognised by a mismatched expiry and skipped.

followups: Each key is rewritten very often, so the heap fills with stale entries. How do you bound its size?
In real JavaScript you would use setTimeout per key instead of a heap. What are the costs of that approach with 100 000 keys?
